title: A Winter for the House
premise: Felix Thackeray hosts a graveyard-shift radio show where callers claim to be listeners who died the previous week; he assumes it's a prank until every photograph of his grandmother's house shows an extra chair, and the chair keeps moving closer to the family. The house is counting its residents, and when the count exceeds the living, the last resident must sign papers transferring ownership to whatever has been waiting in the photographs for generations. Felix, who built his whole identity on being invisible and unattached, must finally claim his found family—his grandmother's odd boarders, a grieving widow named Marisol, and the niece he never knew he had—and get them out ahead of the count before winter solstice, when the last resident signs. He ends by signing the papers himself, but writes his name as 'nobody,' breaking the count, and burns the house's ledger, freeing the dead callers mid-broadcast.
about_author: Rafael Sterling is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent six years answering calls from insomniacs, grief-stricken strangers, and at least one voice he still cannot explain. He writes horror about quiet people who discover that being overlooked is not the same as being safe.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. On the night shift, Felix takes a call from Mrs. Okafor, a devoted listener who died six days ago; he assumes an elaborate prank and plays along on air. The emotional beat is wry detachment masking loneliness—he performs connection nightly but believes in none of it.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Sorting his grandmother Edith's attic photos to digitize them, Felix notices a wooden chair in the background of every image of the house—a chair that appears in photos from 1962 onward, always slightly closer to the front door. Beat: first cold dread beneath his skepticism.

chapters.title: Callers in the Snow
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, intercut with caller transcripts. Three more dead listeners call in, each mentioning 'the house on Corliss Street' unprompted. Felix drives past it at 3 a.m. and sees a light in a window no one lives behind. Beat: skepticism cracking into obsession.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Boarders
chapters.summary: Edith's POV (flashback, 1974). Young Edith takes in her first boarder, a man who signs the ledger without writing a surname. She notices the chair by the door and tells herself it was always there. Beat: tenderness entangled with unease; the house has always collected people.

chapters.title: Marisol at the Door
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A woman named Marisol arrives claiming Edith promised her a room; she's fleeing a marriage that erased her. Reluctantly, Felix lets her stay. That night the chair in the newest photo sits inside the hallway. Beat: reluctant hospitality, the first thread of found family.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. In Edith's study he finds a leather ledger listing every resident of the house since 1908—including names crossed out on dates matching deaths, and a final blank line labeled 'the last resident.' Beat: dread hardens into rules; the house keeps accounts.

chapters.title: Nine Names
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol explores the house and finds nine place settings laid in the dining room though only three people live there. She hears humming from the extra chair. Beat: she chooses to warn Felix rather than flee—the first act of belonging.

chapters.title: The Niece
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. A teenager named Wren shows up with Edith's will: she's Felix's niece, daughter of the brother he hasn't spoken to in fifteen years. The moment she crosses the threshold, the chair in the latest photo moves to the foot of the stairs. Beat: guilt, obligation, unwanted love.

chapters.title: Counting the Living
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix works out the pattern: the chair advances one position per resident added, and when it reaches the table, the last resident signs. He tries sending Wren away, but roads out of town loop back to Corliss Street. Beat: panic under control-freak planning.

chapters.title: What the Callers Know
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, on air. Felix asks his dead callers directly how to stop the count. A voice identifying itself as Edith says only: 'Nobody who stayed invisible ever signed anything worth signing.' Beat: the theme lands—his invisibility is both shield and cage.

chapters.title: Wren Sees It
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren, who photographs everything, captures the chair mid-movement—a smear of something almost human-shaped pulling it forward. She stops sleeping, starts drawing the house obsessively. Beat: the child sees clearly what adults rationalize; fear becomes witness.

chapters.title: The Winter Tenant
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol confronts the presence directly: in the hallway mirror, the reflection shows a gaunt figure seated in the chair, patient, courteous. It asks her, politely, if she'd like to stay forever. Beat: seduction of the house—it offers what each lonely person needs.

chapters.title: Eviction Notice
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix loads everyone into his car and drives until dawn; they arrive back at the house as snow closes over the road behind them. The ledger now lists all their names in fresh ink. Beat: despair—the house doesn't trap you, it simply outlasts your escape.

chapters.title: Edith's Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Edith's voice calls the studio and tells him the truth: she signed as last resident decades ago to protect her boarders, renewing the lease each solstice. This year she died before renewing. The count restarts with whoever lives there now. Beat: love against duty, inherited.

chapters.title: The Papers on the Table
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. On the solstice eve, the transfer papers appear on the dining table beside ten place settings. The chair stands at the table's head. Whoever signs becomes the house's permanent resident, keeping the others safe but bound. Beat: the trap revealed as a bargain.

chapters.title: Everyone Tries to Sign First
chapters.summary: Rotating POV: Marisol, then Wren, then Felix. Each secretly attempts to sign alone and sacrifice themselves; each finds the pen refuses—only the last resident may sign, and the house decides who that is. Beat: devastating tenderness; they've become a family willing to die for each other.

chapters.title: Solstice
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Longest night. The house goes dark room by room, the dead callers broadcasting the countdown over Felix's own signal. The chair pulls itself to the table. Felix realizes the house counts residents—but it has never counted someone who refuses to be counted. Beat: revelation through surrender.

chapters.title: Nobody Signs Here
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. Felix signs the papers 'Nobody Thackeray'—claiming the role while refusing the name, declaring himself uncountable because he belongs to people, not to places. The ledger rejects the entry; the count breaks. Beat: identity theme resolved—visibility chosen, invisibility weaponized.

chapters.title: Burning the Book
chapters.summary: Marisol and Wren's POV. While the house convulses, Marisol holds the mirror-shade at bay with salt and Wren's photographs, and Felix feeds the ledger into the fireplace. The dead callers' voices rise through the radio like a choir. Beat: climax—found family fighting as one unit.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Felix's POV. At dawn, Felix broadcasts one final show, taking calls from the newly freed dead—goodbyes, forgiveness, Mrs. Okafor thanking him for listening. Then he signs off forever. Beat: catharsis; the man who faked connection finally gave it truly.

chapters.title: Spring at Corliss Street
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Weeks later, the three of them remain in the house—not trapped, but staying by choice. New photographs show eleven chairs around the table, all empty, all at rest. Beat: warmth after horror; home rebuilt on chosen bonds.

chapters.title: A Winter for the House
chapters.summary: Felix's POV, epilogue. A new listener calls the revived daytime show asking about a house that counts; Felix smiles, gives honest advice—get your people out ahead of the count—and hangs up. In the corner of the studio, faintly, a chair scrapes closer. Beat: quiet, earned chill; the story breathes but never quite ends.
